rows.question: i have [[Hardened Scales]] and [[Doubling Season]] and cast ballista for X=2. how many counters does it come in with? do i get to pick the order or is it timestamps
rows.expected_answer: You choose the order and the best answer is 6. Walking Ballista's 'enters with X +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect (614.1c, 614.12), and Hardened Scales and Doubling Season are further replacement effects modifying the same event. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected permanent's controller picks which applies first (616.1), and since none of the special priorities in 616.1a-d apply, any may be chosen (616.1e). Each effect applies only once to the event (614.5). Apply Scales first (2 -> 3), then Season doubles (3 -> 6). Timestamps are irrelevant for replacement effects; that is the layer system for continuous effects.

outcome.answer:
You pick the order, not timestamps. Apply **Hardened Scales** first and then **Doubling Season** for the most: 2 → 3 → 6 counters. Doing it the other way gives 2 → 4 → 5.

**Walking Ballista**'s "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it" is a replacement effect (614.1c). Both enchantments apply to it: Hardened Scales enters with "that many plus one" counters, and Doubling Season "affects permanents that enter with counters" (per their Scryfall rulings). Neither enchantment is a self-replacement effect, and neither changes control, copying or which face is up. So under 616.1e you, as the controller of the affected object, may choose either one to apply first. Once it's applied, the other one still applies to the modified event (616.1f).

Timestamps don't matter here. The Hardened Scales ruling spells it out: "you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."

The Ballista's own "enters with X counters" is the event being modified, so it isn't competing with the enchantments. Put Scales before Season and it enters as a 6/6.
citations: rule 616.1: "the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below"
rule 616.1e: "Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen."

rule 616.1f: "Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated (taking into account only replacement or prevention effects that would now be applicable) until there are no more left to apply."
rule 614.1c: "Effects that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ,” “As [this permanent] enters . . . ,” or “[This permanent] enters as . . . “ are replacement effects."
ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/636b245ed2960105: "you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."
ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/86e5ac2af77f77bf: "If a creature you control would enter the battlefield with a number of +1/+1 counters on it, it enters with that many plus one instead."
ruling 01546b7d-a233-4176-8843-d732074dc5b6/30e1af27509ea83b: "Doubling Season affects permanents that enter with counters."

rows.question: opp cast [[Blood Moon]] while i have all three tron lands out. do i still get my 7 mana from urza's? can i tap tower for 3 colorless or is it just a Mountain now
rows.expected_answer: Tron is off. Blood Moon is a type-changing effect (layer 4, 613.1d) that sets each nonbasic land's subtype to Mountain. Per 305.7, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type loses its old land types (so it is no longer an Urza's land), loses all abilities from its rules text (the colorless mana ability), and gains only '{T}: Add {R}'. Each Urza's land is a plain Mountain that taps for one red mana; Tower does not produce three because it no longer has that ability and the others no longer have the Urza's subtype. They are still nonbasic (305.8), so Blood Moon keeps affecting them.

outcome.answer:
No. Under **Blood Moon** each Tron land is just a Mountain. Each one taps only for {R}, so you get 3 red mana, not 7, and **Urza's Tower** cannot make {C}{C}{C}.

Blood Moon's text is "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." The Urza's lands are nonbasic, so this applies to all three. It is a type-changing effect, which is applied in layer 4 (`613.1d`). Per the Blood Moon ruling, affected lands "will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability "{T}: Add {R}."" That removes two things at once:

• The Tower's printed ability ("{T}: Add {C}. If you control an Urza's Mine and an Urza's Power-Plant, add {C}{C}{C} instead.") is gone, and so are the Mine's and Power Plant's.
• The subtypes Urza's Tower, Urza's Mine and Urza's Power-Plant are gone too. Even if something let the Tower keep its ability, it "checks for land types, not the names of other permanents you control", so it would no longer see a Mine or a Power-Plant.

The names stay the same and the lands stay nonbasic, but that doesn't matter here. To get Tron mana back, you need to remove Blood Moon.
citations: oracle 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae#0: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains."

ruling 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae/de7b24c7cfc8d0d2: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability \"{T}: Add {R}.\""
rule 613.1d: "Layer 4: Type-changing effects are applied. These include effects that change an object’s card type, subtype, and/or supertype."
ruling 32fbb638-ab14-4e8b-a07a-d4c44e3496f2/67514ffa8ee40389: "The ability checks for land types, not the names of other permanents you control."

rows.question: follow up: what if I play [[Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth]] AFTER the moon is already down? urborg has the later timestamp so shouldn't it make everything a Swamp too? my friend says no
rows.expected_answer: Your friend is right. Both effects are layer 4 type-changing effects (613.1d). Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's (613.8a): applying Blood Moon makes Urborg a Mountain and strips its rules-text ability (305.7), which removes the existence of Urborg's effect. When a dependency exists it overrides timestamps (613.8), so Blood Moon applies first no matter which entered later (613.8b). Urborg is just a Mountain with '{T}: Add {R}' and nothing becomes a Swamp. (Any actual basic Swamps you control are still Swamps because Blood Moon only affects nonbasic lands.)

outcome.answer:
Your friend is right. Even if **Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth** comes down after **Blood Moon**, no land becomes a Swamp. The only thing Urborg does is tap for {R}.

Why: both "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" and Urborg's "Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types" are type-changing effects, so both apply in layer 4. Normally layer 4 effects apply in timestamp order. But per `613.8`, "If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system."

Urborg's effect depends on Blood Moon's. Per `613.8a`, that's the case when applying the other effect "would change the text or the existence of the first effect." Urborg is a nonbasic land. When Blood Moon sets its land type to Mountain, it "loses all abilities generated from its rules text" (`305.7`), and that includes the Swamp ability. So Blood Moon applies first, per `613.8b`. Once it has, Urborg's effect no longer exists and never applies. Its later timestamp doesn't matter.

Urborg's own ruling says the same: an effect like this "won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply." Urborg does stay legendary, since Blood Moon doesn't touch supertypes. It's just a legendary Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}." Your basic lands aren't Swamps either.
citations: rule 613.8: "If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system."
rule 613.8a: "applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to"
rule 613.8b: "An effect dependent on one or more other effects waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied."

rule 305.7: "It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type."
ruling db6174d7-211d-4817-b8e4-8384594c83f9/aebb4d57471c5c28: "it won't turn lands into Swamps, no matter in what order those effects started to apply."

rows.question: my goyf has two +1/+1 counters on it and I just giant growthed it. opponent [[Clone]]s it. is their clone a huge goyf too or just a regular one? and does the clone even know how big a goyf should be since the p/t is */*+1
rows.expected_answer: Just a regular Tarmogoyf. A copy acquires only the copiable values of the original (707.2): name, mana cost, types, rules text, printed P/T, etc. Counters, Giant Growth's +3/+3, and other non-copy effects are not copiable values, so the Clone gets none of them. The Clone does copy Tarmogoyf's rules text, and therefore its characteristic-defining ability (707.2a), so the Clone's own P/T is */*+1 computed from card types in graveyards (applied in layer 7a, 613.4a). The copy effect itself is applied in layer 1a (613.2a); your goyf's counters and pump are layer 7c (613.4c) and stay on your goyf only.

outcome.answer:
Their Clone is a plain **Tarmogoyf**. It doesn't get your two +1/+1 counters or the **Giant Growth** bonus. It does copy Tarmogoyf's ability, though, so it counts card types in all graveyards the same way yours does. The two Goyfs will have the same base size, and yours is bigger only because of the counters and the pump.

Why: a copy gets only the copiable values, meaning what's printed on the card as modified by other copy effects. Per 707.2, "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied." The Clone rulings say the same: it doesn't copy "whether it has any counters on it" or "any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness". So the +3/+3 from Giant Growth and your counters stay with your Goyf.

On the */*+1 part: Tarmogoyf's power and toughness come from its rules text, "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1." Per 707.2a, "A copy acquires the abilities of the object it's copying because those values are derived from its rules text." The Clone gets that same ability and works out its own power and toughness from the graveyards, updating as they change.

Example: with 3 card types in graveyards, their Clone is 3/4. Your Goyf is 3/4 +2/+2 from the counters +3/+3 from Giant Growth = 8/9 until end of turn.
citations: rule 707.2: "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied."
rule 707.2a: "A copy acquires the abilities of the object it’s copying because those values are derived from its rules text."

ruling 42226b87-0746-4ebf-9fd0-108d508462af/e115f2763b5d5e7e: "It doesn't copy whether that creature is tapped or untapped, whether it has any counters on it or Auras and Equipment attached to it, or any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness, ty…"
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1."

rows.question: ok classic one. I have [[Humility]] out and my opponent drops [[Opalescence]]. what are Humility and Opalescence now?? are all my creatures still 1/1? does the answer change if Opalescence was out first?
rows.expected_answer: Walk the layers. Opalescence reads 'each OTHER non-Aura enchantment', so it never affects itself: Opalescence stays a noncreature enchantment and keeps its ability in every scenario. Layer 4 (613.1d): Opalescence makes Humility a 'creature' enchantment. Layer 6 (613.1f): Humility removes all abilities from every creature, including itself; per 613.6 an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers even though its source ability is gone. Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility's 'base P/T 1/1' and Opalescence's 'base P/T equal to mana value' both set Humility's P/T. Neither depends on the other under 613.8a (applying one doesn't change the text, existence, or targets of the other), so timestamp order decides (613.7). If Opalescence has the later timestamp: Humility is a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Humility has the later timestamp: Humility is a 1/1 creature with no abilities. Either way every ordinary creature is a 1/1 with no abilities, and Opalescence is an unaffected noncreature enchantment. Any other non-Aura enchantment Opalescence animates follows Humility itself: its base power and toughness are its mana value when Opalescence is later, and 1/1 when Humility is.

outcome.answer:
Your other creatures stay 1/1 with no abilities either way. **Opalescence** says "Each other non-Aura enchantment", so it never becomes a creature itself and keeps its ability. What changes with the order is **Humility**. If Humility came first (your case), it ends up a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Opalescence came first, Humility ends up a 1/1 creature with no abilities.

Here's how the layers go with Humility first:
- Layer 4 (type changes, `613.1d`): Opalescence makes Humility a creature.
- Layer 6 (abilities, `613.1f`): Humility removes all abilities from all creatures, including itself. Per `613.6`, an effect that has started applying "will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable layer and/or sublayer, even if the ability generating the effect is removed." So Humility's 1/1 effect still happens in layer 7b.
- Layer 7b (`613.4b`): both effects set base P/T, so they apply in timestamp order (`613.7`). Humility's 1/1 applies first, then Opalescence's later effect sets Humility to its mana value, 4/4.

If Opalescence came first, layer 7b runs the other way round. Opalescence sets Humility to 4/4, then Humility's later effect sets it back to 1/1. The Scryfall ruling on these two cards goes through exactly this order-by-order breakdown.

One more thing: any other non-Aura enchantments on the battlefield also become creatures and lose their abilities. They follow the same pattern as Humility, so they're 1/1 if Opalescence came first and equal to their mana value if Humility came first.
citations: oracle 59489b46-9d02-4f3c-bcd0-884e7605e9a5#0: "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types"
rule 613.6: "it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable layer and/or sublayer, even if the ability generating the effect is removed during this process."
rule 613.4b: "Layer 7b: Effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value are applied. Effects that refer to the base power and/or toughness of a creature apply in this layer."
rule 613.7: "An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp."
rule 613.1d: "Layer 4: Type-changing effects are applied."
rule 613.1f: "Layer 6: Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that say an object can’t have an ability are applied."
ruling ed7bdb3e-5c51-4547-9266-76a791e0b2b0/18649cad787b2eba: "Layer 7b: Humility becomes 1/1 and Worship becomes 1/1 (Humility). Humility becomes 4/4 and Worship becomes 4/4 (Opalescence)."

rows.question: quick one: if I have [[Valki, God of Lies]] in hand can I just cast the Tibalt side for 7? and while it's in my library/graveyard does it count as a planeswalker card for stuff like Vraska's Contempt / Kaya's Ghostform?
rows.expected_answer: Yes. Valki // Tibalt is a modal double-faced card: when you cast it you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack, and only that face is evaluated (712.11b, 712.11c), so you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for {5}{B}{R} straight from your hand. Once chosen, the spell/permanent has only that face's characteristics (712.8f). But anywhere other than the stack or battlefield (hand, library, graveyard, exile) an MDFC has only its front face's characteristics (712.8a), so it is a legendary creature card named Valki, God of Lies there — never a planeswalker card.

outcome.answer:
Yes, you can cast **Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor** for {5}{B}{R}. In your library or graveyard, though, the card is only **Valki**: a 2-mana legendary creature card, not a planeswalker card.

**Casting:** for a modal double-faced card, you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack (`712.11b`). While Tibalt is on the stack or battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that's up (`712.8f`). So on the battlefield it's a planeswalker, and **Vraska's Contempt** can target it. **Kaya's Ghostform** ("Enchant creature or planeswalker you control") can also enchant it.

**Other zones:** outside the battlefield and stack, a double-faced card has only its front face's characteristics (`712.8a`). In hand, library, graveyard or exile, it's a creature card with mana value 2. Anything checking for a "planeswalker card" there won't see it. Neither Contempt nor Ghostform looks at cards in those zones anyway. They only affect permanents on the battlefield.

**Watch out with Ghostform on Tibalt:** if Tibalt dies or is exiled, Ghostform returns "that card" to the battlefield. A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from anywhere other than the stack enters front face up by default (`712.14`). So you get **Valki** back, not Tibalt. Valki's enters trigger then makes each opponent reveal their hand.
citations: rule 712.11b: "A player casting a modal double-faced card or a copy of a modal double-faced card as a spell chooses which face they are casting before putting it onto the stack."
rule 712.8f: "While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that’s up."
rule 712.8a: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face."
rule 712.14: "A double-faced card put onto the battlefield from a zone other than the stack enters the battlefield with its front face up by default."
ruling 907ae517-22d5-4ac7-bc3a-3f4d5eaeeb57/9ee99cc325b8e973: "If an effect puts a double-faced card onto the battlefield, it enters with its front face up."

rows.question: cast Stomp off my bonecrusher giant, it resolved and went to exile. my opp says I can only cast the creature half from exile now, not Stomp again, is that right? also can they counter Stomp with a 'counter target creature spell' effect since the card is a creature?
rows.expected_answer: Your opponent is right. When an Adventure spell resolves it is exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and you may cast the card from exile — but only as the creature (Bonecrusher Giant), not as Stomp again (715.3d). And no, Stomp can't be hit by 'counter target creature spell': while on the stack as an Adventure the spell has only its alternative characteristics (715.3a, 715.3b), so it is a red instant, not a creature spell. Everywhere else, including exile, the card is just the creature card Bonecrusher Giant (715.4).

outcome.answer:
Your opponent is right about the first part, and no on the second. Once **Stomp** resolves and goes to exile, you can cast **Bonecrusher Giant** from there as the creature, but not as Stomp again. A "counter target creature spell" effect can't target Stomp either.

**Casting from exile:** Per `715.3d`, a spell cast as an Adventure is exiled as it resolves, and "For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can't be cast as an Adventure this way." You still follow the creature's normal timing, so usually only in your main phase while the stack is empty. Another effect that lets you cast cards from exile might let you cast it as an Adventure, but this built-in permission doesn't.

**Countering:** While Stomp is on the stack, per `715.3b` "the spell has only its alternative characteristics." That makes it an instant spell, not a creature spell, so "counter target creature spell" can't target it. The Scryfall rulings say the same: when you cast a spell as an Adventure, you ignore all of the card's normal characteristics. The card goes back to being a creature card only once it leaves the stack. A general "counter target spell" effect can still counter Stomp. If that happens, the card goes to your graveyard instead of exile, and you lose the chance to cast the Giant later.
citations: rule 715.3d: "For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can’t be cast as an Adventure this way"
rule 715.3b: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics."
ruling d6d72f5f-8f5d-4180-b514-f22ff5482902/700df45a4e7078ff: "When casting a spell as an Adventure, use the alternative characteristics and ignore all of the card's normal characteristics."

ruling d6d72f5f-8f5d-4180-b514-f22ff5482902/9f9546560bbab6ce: "If an Adventure spell leaves the stack in any way other than resolving (most likely by being countered or by failing to resolve because its targets have all become illegal), that card won't be exiled"

rows.question: melded my Bruna and Gisela into Brisela and then it got Path to Exiled. does that count as one creature leaving or two for my [[Blood Artist]] type triggers, and do I get one Plains or two off Path?
rows.expected_answer:
Blood Artist does not trigger at all here: Path to Exile exiles Brisela, and Blood Artist
triggers on a creature dying, which means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield
(700.4). Exile is not dying. If Brisela instead died (say, to a Wrath of God), Blood Artist
would trigger exactly once: one permanent left the battlefield, even though the melded
permanent is a single object represented by two cards (712.21, 701.42a). A trigger reading
"whenever a card is put into a graveyard" would see two cards (712.21e). Either way, the
search happens once and Bruna and Gisela both go to exile. It is Brisela's controller who
searches, not the player who cast Path to Exile ("Its controller may search their library
for a basic land card"), and any basic land will do, not only a Plains.

outcome.answer:
**Brisela** is one creature leaving the battlefield, so you get one basic land off **Path to Exile**. **Blood Artist** doesn't trigger at all here, because Brisela was exiled, not killed.

Per `712.21`, when a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves and two cards go to the new zone. Brisela was a single creature, so Path does its thing once: "Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle." That's one search for one land, even though two cards (Bruna and Gisela) end up in exile.

Blood Artist says "Whenever this creature or another creature dies", and per `700.4` "dies" means "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield." Exile isn't a graveyard, so there's no trigger. If Brisela had died instead, Blood Artist would trigger only once: per `712.21e`, a melded permanent counts as one object that moved. It only counts as two for effects that count *cards* changing zones, like "whenever a card is put into a graveyard" triggers.
citations: rule 712.21: "If a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone."
rule 712.21e: "If an effect needs to know the number of objects that changed zones, a melded permanent among those objects counts as one object that moved."
rule 700.4: "The term dies means “is put into a graveyard from the battlefield.”"
oracle d683d985-9888-4d21-8b5f-69e69ce4a03b#0: "Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle."

rows.question: old school question. my Waylay (Urza's Saga printing) says 'at end of turn, remove them from the game'. so I cast it during my opponent's end step, the knights survive since the end step already started, and I get to swing with them on my turn right? classic waylay trick
rows.expected_answer: No — that trick was closed by errata. The printed text is not what the card does; you always use the current Oracle wording (108.1), which is 'Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step.' If you cast Waylay in your opponent's end step, the Knights are exiled at that same turn's cleanup step: the game checks for triggered abilities waiting during cleanup, puts the 'beginning of the next cleanup step' trigger on the stack, and then players get priority and another cleanup step follows (514.3a). You never get to attack with them. (Casting it during your opponent's declare-attackers step to get surprise blockers still works.)

outcome.answer:
No, that trick doesn't work anymore. **Waylay** has been errata'd. Its current Oracle text reads "Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step." The old "at end of turn" wording is gone.

When Waylay resolves, it creates a delayed triggered ability (`603.7`) that waits for the next cleanup step. That's the very next step of the same turn, because "The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup" (`512.1`). Starting in the end step doesn't help you: `513.2`'s "the step doesn't back up" rule only covers end-step triggers, and this one is waiting for cleanup.

In that cleanup step, the game checks for triggered abilities waiting to go on the stack, "including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”" (`514.3a`). The trigger goes on the stack and resolves, and the Knights are exiled. Then another cleanup step begins.

So the Knights last only for the rest of your opponent's end step. They're fine as sacrifice fodder, or as surprise blockers if you cast Waylay earlier in the turn, but they never make it to your turn.
citations: oracle f0db78c7-09b5-4981-8ca8-6dbab597c5d9#0: "Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step."
rule 603.7: "An effect may create a delayed triggered ability that can do something at a later time."
rule 512.1: "The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup."
rule 514.3a: "including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”"
rule 513.2: "Likewise, if a delayed triggered ability that triggers “at the beginning of the next end step” is created during this step, that ability won’t trigger until the next turn’s end step."

rows.question: my mirage LED says 'play this ability as an interrupt'. so it's a mana ability and I can crack it in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor to pay for it right? that way I still have tutor as the last card when I discard
rows.expected_answer: No. Ignore the printed 'interrupt' text and use the current Oracle wording (108.1): 'Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant.' It is still a mana ability — the timing restriction doesn't change that (605.1) — but 'Activate only as an instant' means you may only activate it when you have priority (602.5e), so you can't activate it while paying for a spell the way 605.3a normally allows for mana abilities. The correct play is to cast Infernal Tutor with Tutor as the last card in hand, hold priority, then activate LED in response; when Tutor resolves you are hellbent and the mana is still floating.

outcome.answer:
No. **Lion's Eye Diamond** can't be activated in the middle of casting **Infernal Tutor**. The old "interrupt" wording doesn't apply. Use the current Oracle text: "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant."

It is still a mana ability. Per `605.1`, an ability counts as a mana ability no matter what timing restriction it has. But per `602.5e`, "Activate only as an instant" means you have to follow instant timing. The Scryfall ruling agrees: it "can only be activated at times when you can cast an instant." Normally a mana ability can be activated partway through casting a spell (`605.3a`). While you're casting a spell, though, you can't cast an instant, so LED can't be used to pay for Tutor. You only get priority again after the spell is cast (`601.2i`).

Your plan also wouldn't do what you want. As soon as you start casting Tutor, it moves to the stack (`601.2a`), so it's no longer in your hand when you'd discard.

The correct line: pay for Infernal Tutor with other mana and hold priority. Then, with Tutor on the stack, activate LED in response. Your hand is now empty, so when Tutor resolves, Hellbent applies: "If you have no cards in hand, instead search your library for a card, put it into your hand, then shuffle." You'll also have three mana floating to spend on the card you find during that same step.
citations: oracle ee6099b0-fb1f-42f1-b862-7708c6e36d05#0: "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant."

rows.question: ok so I have [[Blood Artist]] out and my opponent wraths with [[Wrath of God]]. Blood Artist dies at the same time as everything else so does it even see the other creatures die? do I drain for all of them or just itself?
rows.expected_answer: Yes, you drain for every creature that died, including Blood Artist itself. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities 'look back in time' (603.10, 603.6c): the game checks the state immediately before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield, so it sees every creature that died simultaneously, including itself. All those triggers go on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3), and you choose a target player for each one.

outcome.answer:
Yes. **Blood Artist** triggers once for itself and once for every other creature that dies to **Wrath of God**, so you drain for all of them.

The reason is that "dies" triggers look back in time. Per `603.6c`, an ability that triggers on something being "put into a graveyard from the battlefield" is a leaves-the-battlefield ability. Per `603.10a`, those look back in time: the game checks for them using how things were just before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield alongside everything else. The example under `603.10` is basically your case: an artifact with "Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life" gets destroyed along with two creatures, and its ability still triggers twice.

Per `603.2c`, one event with several occurrences triggers the ability once for each occurrence. The Blood Artist ruling says the same: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."

You control every trigger. Each one has you pick a target player to lose 1 life, and you gain 1 life each time.
citations: rule 603.10a: "Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities"
rule 603.6c: "“Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .”"
rule 603.10: "The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures."
rule 603.2c: "However, it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences."
ruling 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d/eaf0e0e76c3621ab: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."

rows.question: my buddy says once I cast a spell he can't respond until I 'pass'. I cast Lightning Bolt at his bob, do I get to keep going and cast a second Bolt before he gets a chance to counter the first one?
rows.expected_answer: Your buddy is half right. After you cast a spell you receive priority again (117.3c), so you may cast the second Bolt immediately, before he can respond to the first. He only gets priority when you pass. Nothing resolves until all players pass in succession with the stack non-empty (117.4); then only the top object resolves, and the active player gets priority again after it resolves (117.3b). So he can still respond to either Bolt once you pass, but you are entitled to stack both first.

outcome.answer:
Yes. After you cast a spell, you get priority back, so you can cast the second **Lightning Bolt** right away, before your buddy gets a chance to do anything. Per `117.3c`, "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward." Your opponent only gets priority when you pass. Under `117.3d`, if you choose not to take any action, you pass, and "Then the next player in turn order receives priority."

Once both Bolts are on the stack and you pass, your buddy can still respond, and he can counter either Bolt, the first one included. Casting the second Bolt doesn't lock the first one in. It only means the second Bolt is "in response to" the first, so it resolves first if nobody changes anything (`117.7`).

One caution for aiming both Bolts at **Dark Confidant**: if the Bolt on top kills it, the other Bolt has no legal target when it tries to resolve. Per `608.2b`, it "doesn't resolve" and goes to your graveyard. Only stack two Bolts on the same creature if you actually need both.
citations: rule 117.3c: "If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward."
rule 117.3d: "If a player has priority and chooses not to take any actions, that player passes."
rule 117.7: "the new spell or ability has been cast or activated “in response to” the earlier spell or ability. The new spell or ability will resolve first."
rule 608.2b: "If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve."

rows.question: I control a 2/2 with a Giant Growth resolving on it, and mid-resolution of a different spell it's technically at 0 toughness for a second (Maro-style hand-size thing). Does it die? And separately, if I have two Ragavan on the battlefield somehow, when exactly does the legend rule kick in - can I respond in between?
rows.expected_answer: 1) It doesn't die. State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, not in the middle of a spell resolving (704.3, 704.4 - the CR's own Maro example). The creature only dies if it still has toughness 0 or less when SBAs are next checked (704.5f). 2) The legend rule (704.5j) is also a state-based action: the moment a player would get priority with two Ragavans you control, you choose one and the other goes to the graveyard. It doesn't use the stack and there is no window to respond between the second Ragavan entering and the legend rule applying; you can only respond before the second one enters/resolves.

outcome.answer:
**Your 2/2:** it survives, as long as its toughness is back above 0 when the spell finishes resolving. Nothing checks toughness in the middle of a resolution. The game only looks for state-based actions when a player would get priority (704.3), and per 704.4 "state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability." The **Maro** ruling makes the same point: if toughness drops to 0 during a resolution and comes back up before that resolution ends, the creature isn't put into the graveyard. (If the Giant Growth has already resolved, your creature is a 5/5 until end of turn anyway.) It only dies if its toughness is still 0 or less once the spell has finished and state-based actions are checked (704.5f).

**Two Ragavans:** no, you can't respond between the second Ragavan arriving and the legend rule. The legend rule is a state-based action (704.5j): you choose one Ragavan and the other goes to the graveyard. State-based actions don't use the stack (704.1), and they're handled before any player would receive priority (117.2d). So the moment the second **Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer** is on the battlefield, the next state-based action check removes one before anyone can act. Your only window is while the second Ragavan is still a spell on the stack. At that point only one is on the battlefield, so you can still use the first one, or sacrifice or bounce it, before the second resolves.
citations: rule 704.4: "Unlike triggered abilities, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability."
rule 704.3: "Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, “Timing and Priority”), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions"

ruling ef32258a-d567-4fbc-ab85-8c00080f5b36/654c63e82671903c: "If Maro’s toughness goes to 0 during the announcement or resolution of a spell or ability and then goes back up above 0 before the end of that announcement or resolution, it won’t be put into your gra…"
rule 704.5f: "If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard."
rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards."
rule 704.1: "State-based actions don’t use the stack."
rule 117.2d: "They’re dealt with before a player would receive priority."

rows.question: I attack with a 5/5 trample that also has deathtouch (Questing Beast) and they block with a 4/4. how much can I trample over? my opponent says I have to assign 4 to the blocker first
rows.expected_answer: The premise is off: Questing Beast is a 4/4 with vigilance, deathtouch and haste, and it does not have trample, so blocked by one creature it assigns all its combat damage to that blocker and nothing goes to the player (510.1c). A good answer says so. For the creature the asker describes, a 5/5 with trample and deathtouch, you only need to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 and can trample 4 over to the player. Trample requires lethal damage to be assigned to all blockers before excess goes to the player (702.19b), but any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that purpose (702.2c). Damage assignment for a blocked creature follows 510.1c, then all combat damage is dealt simultaneously with no chance to respond in between (510.2). The 4/4 is then destroyed by deathtouch as an SBA.

outcome.answer:
You can trample over **4**. Assign just 1 damage to the 4/4 and 4 to the player. Your opponent is wrong here: deathtouch changes what counts as lethal damage.

Per `702.19b`, a trampler has to assign lethal damage to its blockers before any excess can go to the player. But per `702.2c`, "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage" for that check. So 1 damage covers the 4/4's lethal requirement and the other 4 is excess. That 1 damage still destroys the blocker as a state-based action (`702.2b`).

One thing to check: **Questing Beast**'s Oracle text doesn't give it trample ("Vigilance, deathtouch, haste"). It needs trample from some other effect. Without trample, a blocked creature assigns all its damage to its blocker (`510.1c`).

As a bonus, the 4 damage to your opponent triggers "it deals that much damage to target planeswalker that player controls," if they control one.
citations: rule 702.19b: "Once all those blocking creatures are assigned lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as its controller chooses among those blocking creatures and the player, planeswalker, or battle the creatur…"

rule 702.2c: "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt."
rule 702.2b: "A creature with toughness greater than 0 that’s been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last time state-based actions were checked is destroyed as a state-based action."
oracle b685757b-521e-4353-a233-97052359723d#0: "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste"
rule 510.1c: "If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature."

rows.question: commander q: my commander is [[Kenrith, the Returned King]]. two things: 1) can I run Nicol Bolas, the Ravager since Kenrith's text mentions all 5 colors? and 2) someone bounced Kenrith to my hand with Unsummon - does he go to the command zone or is that only for graveyard/exile?
rows.expected_answer: 1) Yes. Color identity includes mana symbols in the mana cost AND in the rules text (903.4), so Kenrith's identity is WUBRG even though his mana cost is only {4}{W}. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager (UBR) is legal because every color in its identity is in Kenrith's (903.5c). 2) Yes, Kenrith can go to the command zone. If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead - a replacement effect (903.9b). Graveyard/exile use a separate state-based action (903.9a). Either way it's optional.

outcome.answer:
1) **Yes.** **Kenrith, the Returned King**'s color identity is all five colors, so **Nicol Bolas, the Ravager** is legal in the deck. 2) **Yes, you may put Kenrith into the command zone instead of your hand.** This replacement works for hand and library as well as graveyard and exile.

**1:** Per `903.4`, color identity counts the mana symbols in a card's mana cost *and* its rules text. Kenrith costs {4}{W}, and his abilities include {R}, {G}, {U} and {B} (for example "{4}{B}: Put target creature card from a graveyard onto the battlefield"). That makes his identity W/U/B/R/G. Nicol Bolas is blue, black and red. His back face also counts (`903.4d`), but the Arisen's color indicator only adds those same three colors. Per `903.5c`, a card can be in the deck if every color in its identity is also in your commander's identity, and that's true here.

**2:** **Unsummon** says "Return target creature to its owner's hand." Per `903.9b`, if a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, the owner may put it into the command zone instead. This is a replacement, so Kenrith never reaches your hand. You can also let him go to your hand and cast him from there with no commander tax, since tax only applies to casting from the command zone. The separate check for graveyard/exile (`903.9a`) is a state-based action; hand and library use the replacement.
citations: rule 903.4: "The color identity of a card is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text"
rule 903.4d: "The back face of a double-faced card (see rule 712) is included when determining a card’s color identity."
rule 903.5c: "A card can be included in a Commander deck only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck’s commander."
rule 903.9b: "If a commander would be put into its owner’s hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead."
rule 903.9a: "If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone."

oracle 837182db-1bf3-4a2c-bd01-1af9d9873561#0: "Return target creature to its owner's hand."

rows.question: commander damage question. I've been hit for 15 by my opponent's Rafiq. she then copies it with a Clone and hits me for 6 more with the clone. do I lose? also does the 21 count noncombat damage like from Fling?
rows.expected_answer: No to both. A player loses when they've been dealt 21 or more COMBAT damage by the SAME commander over the course of the game (903.10a; checked as a state-based action, 704.6c). The Clone copying Rafiq is not a commander, so its 6 damage isn't commander damage - you're still at 15 from the real Rafiq. Fling damage is noncombat, so it never counts toward the 21 either; it just reduces your life total normally.

outcome.answer:
No, you don't lose. Only damage from her actual **Rafiq of the Many** counts toward the 21. The **Clone**'s 6 is ordinary damage: you still lose 6 life, but it adds nothing to Rafiq's 15.

The rule you're thinking of is 903.10a: a player loses if they've "been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game." Being a commander is an attribute of the card itself, not a copiable characteristic (903.3). So the Clone copies Rafiq's name, text and stats, but it is not a commander. 903.3 says so directly: "A permanent that's copying a commander ... is not a commander." If she attacks with the real Rafiq later, that damage keeps adding to the 15.

On **Fling**: no, noncombat damage never counts. 903.10a only counts *combat* damage dealt by a commander. It also doesn't matter what she sacrifices to Fling, even Rafiq itself: the damage is dealt by Fling, not by the commander, and it isn't combat damage. It just costs you life as normal.
citations: rule 903.10a: "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game."
rule 903.3: "This designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself."
rule 903.3: "A permanent that’s copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player’s graveyard) is not a commander."
oracle 24227761-b50e-4b9e-93a2-e82d053b3e3d#0: "Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature's power to any target."

rows.question: two quick ones. 1) if I tap all my lands during my upkeep does that mana stick around so I can cast the mind sculptor in my main phase? 2) when I'm casting snappy can I tap lands in the middle of casting it or do I have to float the mana first?
rows.expected_answer: 1) No. Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, so mana added during your upkeep is lost before your main phase (106.4). Tap the lands in your main phase instead. 2) Yes. Casting a spell includes a step where, if the total cost includes mana, you get a chance to activate mana abilities such as tapping lands (601.2g), and only then do you pay the total cost (601.2h). You do not need to float mana before announcing the spell.

outcome.answer:
1) No. Mana you add during your upkeep drains away before your main phase. Per `106.4`, "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase". The upkeep is its own step of the beginning phase (`501.1`), so that mana is gone before the draw step even starts. You'd have to spend it during upkeep, and you can't cast **Jace, the Mind Sculptor** then anyway because it isn't an instant. Tap your lands in your main phase instead.

2) You can tap lands while you're casting it. There's no need to float mana first. Casting a spell follows the steps in `601.2`. After the total cost is locked in, `601.2g` says you "then [have] a chance to activate mana abilities", and you pay in `601.2h`. Tapping a land for mana is a mana ability (`605.1a`), and `605.3a` lets you activate one "whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment". So you put **Snapcaster Mage** on the stack, then tap lands to pay for it. The same goes for flashback costs you pay later with its trigger.
citations: rule 106.4: "Each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana."
rule 501.1: "The beginning phase consists of three steps, in this order: untap, upkeep, and draw."

rule 601.2g: "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid."
rule 601.2h: "The player pays the total cost."

rule 605.1a: "An activated ability is a mana ability if it meets all of the following criteria: it doesn’t require a target (see rule 115.6), it could add mana to a player’s mana pool when it resolves"
rule 605.3a: "A player may activate an activated mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment"
rule 601.2: "To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order."

rows.question: my opp has [[bob]] and flipped a tim off the top, then next turn he flipped a goyf. how much life does he lose each time? goyf is like a 5/6 rn so is it 5?
rows.expected_answer: Dark Confidant makes you lose life equal to the revealed card's mana value, which is the total mana in its mana cost regardless of color (202.3). Prodigal Sorcerer costs {2}{U}, so he loses 3 life. Tarmogoyf costs {1}{G}, so he loses 2 life. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness is irrelevant; mana value is based only on the mana cost.

outcome.answer:
He loses **3** life for the Tim and **2** for the Goyf. Goyf's power doesn't matter, so it isn't 5.

**Dark Confidant** says "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value." Mana value is the total mana in the card's mana cost, whatever the colors (`202.3`).

**Prodigal Sorcerer** (Tim) costs {2}{U}, so its mana value is 3.

**Tarmogoyf** costs {1}{G}, so its mana value is 2. Its ability only sets power and toughness ("Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards..."). It doesn't touch the mana cost. Goyf can be 5/6 and Bob still only takes 2.
citations: rule 202.3: "The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color."
oracle 2068185c-1b50-47d0-aa3f-bf505d199428#0: "reveal the top card of your library and put that card into your hand. You lose life equal to its mana value."
oracle 45900b2f-f6a9-4c42-9642-008f3c1cf6dd#0: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards"
